# STM32H743 FC + 80A 4-in-1 ESC: Power, Thermal & DShot Architecture (Job #9)

## 0. Assumptions and Scope

No MOSFET part number, board stack-up, or burst duration was given. The numbers below therefore come from **stated, representative parameters**. Every equation is parametric, so you can substitute datasheet values when the BOM is frozen.

**Architectural note:** In a FC + 4-in-1 stack, the 48 kHz PWM is generated by the **ESC's own MCU** (e.g., AT32F421 or STM32G071 running AM32 or BLHeli_32), not by the H743. The H743 only sources bidirectional DShot600 and captures eRPM telemetry. The model is split along that boundary.

| Parameter | Symbol | Assumed value |
|---|---|---|
| Battery (6S, full) | V_bus | 25.2 V |
| Burst phase current, per motor | I_pk | 80 A |
| PWM frequency | f_sw | 48 kHz |
| MOSFET R_DS(on) @ 25 °C, V_GS = 10 V | R_25 | 1.2 mΩ (40 V, 3.3×3.3 PQFN class) |
| R_DS(on) temperature coefficient | α | 0.0045 /K |
| Rise + fall time at 80 A | t_r + t_f | 20 + 20 ns |
| Output capacitance (effective) | C_oss | 1.5 nF |
| Reverse recovery charge | Q_rr | 40 nC |
| Total gate charge | Q_g | 50 nC @ 10 V |
| Dead time | t_d | 300 ns per edge |
| Body-diode forward voltage | V_f | 0.8 V |
| Current shunt (per motor) | R_sh | 0.5 mΩ |
| Copper path resistance, per motor | R_cu | 0.4 mΩ |
| Board form factor | — | 30.5×30.5 mm, 6-layer, 2 oz outer / 2 oz inner |

> ⚠️ **Feasibility flag:** 80 A per motor on a 20×20 "nano" board is not thermally credible beyond sub-second transients (see §3). This design assumes the 30.5×30.5 form factor. Labeling a 20×20 board "80 A" would be a burst-only marketing figure.

---

## 1. Conduction Loss Model

### 1.1 Current path
In trapezoidal six-step commutation with synchronous rectification, current always flows through **two conducting device positions**:
- the PWM'd phase leg (high-side during D, synchronous low-side during 1−D), and
- the static low-side of the return phase.

Ignoring ripple, the RMS-equivalent loss per motor is:

$$P_{cond} = I^2\left[2R_{DS}(T_j) + R_{sh} + R_{cu}\right]$$

Ripple correction (triangular ripple ΔI):

$$I_{rms}^2 = I^2 + \frac{\Delta I^2}{12}$$

ΔI is typically 5–15 A at 48 kHz with low-inductance drone motors. This adds less than 0.3 %, so it is neglected.

### 1.2 Temperature-dependent R_DS(on)

$$R_{DS}(T_j) = R_{25}\left[1+\alpha(T_j-25)\right]$$

At T_j = 110 °C:

$$R_{DS} = 1.2\,\text{m}\Omega \times (1 + 0.0045 \times 85) = 1.66\,\text{m}\Omega$$

### 1.3 Numbers at 80 A

| Term | Calculation | Loss |
|---|---|---|
| MOSFETs | 6400 × 2 × 1.66 mΩ | **21.2 W** |
| Shunt | 6400 × 0.5 mΩ | 3.2 W |
| Copper | 6400 × 0.4 mΩ | 2.6 W |
| **Conduction total per motor** | | **27.0 W** |

**Per-FET average.** Each of the 6 FETs carries current about 1/3 of the electrical cycle, in different roles. MOSFET conduction loss per FET is therefore about 21.2 / 6 ≈ **3.5 W average**. The instantaneous loss of a conducting FET is I²R = 10.6 W.

### 1.4 Thermal runaway check
R_DS(on) rises with T_j, so loss and temperature feed back on each other. Solving for the steady state:

$$T_j = T_a + R_{th,ja}\,P_0\left[1+\alpha(T_j-25)\right]$$

$$T_j = \frac{T_a + R_{th}P_0(1-25\alpha)}{1-\alpha R_{th}P_0}$$

The solution is stable only if:

$$\alpha R_{th}P_0 < 1$$

For P₀ = 2.5 W (the per-FET average at 25 °C), the condition requires R_th,ja < 89 K/W. That is easily met, so runaway is not a risk. The real risk is the **board-level energy budget** in §3.

## 2. Switching Loss Model at 48 kHz

Only the PWM'd leg switches: one high-side/low-side pair per motor at any instant.

### 2.1 Hard-switching V–I overlap

$$P_{VI} = \tfrac12 V_{bus} I (t_r+t_f) f_{sw}$$

$$= 0.5 \times 25.2 \times 80 \times 40\,\text{ns} \times 48\,\text{kHz} = \mathbf{1.94\ W}$$

### 2.2 Output capacitance

$$P_{oss} = C_{oss} V^2 f_{sw}$$

The factor is ½ per edge × 2 devices. Result: 1.5 nF × 635 × 48 kHz = **0.046 W**.

### 2.3 Reverse recovery (sync FET body diode)

$$P_{rr} = Q_{rr} V f_{sw} = 40\,\text{nC} \times 25.2 \times 48\,\text{kHz} = \mathbf{0.048\ W}$$

The recovery current also adds to high-side turn-on loss, roughly +0.1–0.3 W. Measure this on a double-pulse fixture.

### 2.4 Dead-time body-diode conduction

$$P_{dt} = V_f I (2t_d) f_{sw} = 0.8 \times 80 \times 600\,\text{ns} \times 48\,\text{kHz} = \mathbf{1.84\ W}$$

> **Key finding:** Dead-time loss is about the same size as the V–I overlap loss. Reducing dead time from 300 ns to 100 ns in AM32 (if your gate driver's propagation matching allows it) saves about **1.2 W per motor** at 80 A.

### 2.5 Gate drive (dissipated in the driver/resistors, not the FET)

$$P_g = 2 Q_g V_{GS} f_{sw} = 2 \times 50\,\text{nC} \times 10 \times 48\,\text{kHz} = 0.048\ \text{W}$$

### 2.6 Switching summary per motor

| Term | Loss |
|---|---|
| V–I overlap | 1.94 W |
| Dead-time diode | 1.84 W |
| Q_rr + C_oss + gate | 0.14 W |
| Q_rr turn-on margin | 0.2 W |
| **Switching total** | **≈ 4.1 W** |

**Frequency trade-off:** P_sw scales linearly with f_sw.
- 24 kHz: about 2.1 W, but more audible noise, higher current ripple, and worse low-throttle resolution.
- 96 kHz: about 8.2 W.

48 kHz is a reasonable compromise.
